name: Veerateswarar Temple, Keelaparasalur
deity: Shiva as Veerateswarar (Daksha Samhara Murti), with the goddess Ilam Kobanayal
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam and one of the Ashta Veerattanam
summary: Keelaparasalur, near Mayiladuthurai, is one of the eight Ashta Veerattanam shrines, each marking a heroic deed of Shiva. Here the lord is worshipped as Veerateswarar, in the form in which he quelled the sacrifice of Daksha — the father-in-law who denied him his due — so the place is also called Dakshapuram, and the temple Dakshapureeswarar. A Paadal Petra Sthalam sung in the Tevaram, with the goddess Ilam Kobanayal, it joins the Tamil saints' devotion to one of Shaiva tradition's great mythic reckonings.

sections.history: Keelaparasalur, whose historical name is Tirupparialur, is an ancient Shaiva village near Mayiladuthurai, hymned in the seventh-century Tevaram by Sambandar and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Kaveri's southern bank. Its special standing is as one of the Ashta Veerattanam — the eight shrines, each tied to one of Shiva's heroic deeds. The stone temple is of the Chola period; the village's alternate name, Dakshapuram, keeps alive its identity as the field of the Daksha episode.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan with a gopuram, prakara and the sanctum of Veerateswarar; the goddess is worshipped as Ilam Kobanayal (also called Balambika). As a veerattanam temple, its iconography and worship hold the memory of Shiva's reckoning with Daksha, and the form of the lord as Daksha Samhara Murti is central to the sacred image the pilgrim comes to see.
sections.legends: The legend that defines Keelaparasalur is the sacrifice of Daksha. In the tradition, Daksha held a great yagna but denied his son-in-law Shiva the honour due to him; Shiva's consort, going to the sacrifice against his wish, could not bear the insult, and in the aftermath Shiva's wrath — through his fierce aspect — brought the sacrifice to an end and chastened Daksha, who was later restored and reconciled. From this heroic act the lord is worshipped here as Veerateswarar, and the place remembered as Dakshapuram.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham, the Margazhi season and the annual Brahmotsavam — and its identity as an Ashta Veerattanam shrine gives weight to the days recalling Shiva's heroic form. Pilgrims completing the circuit of the eight veerattanam temples make a point of worshipping here.
sections.experience: Keelaparasalur is a quiet delta temple whose atmosphere is charged by its myth. Pilgrims come aware that they stand on one of the eight fields of Shiva's valour, and the darshan of Veerateswarar carries the weight of a reckoning that restored right order. For those making the Ashta Veerattanam pilgrimage, it is an essential stop.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Keelaparasalur is about 13 km from Mayiladuthurai in Mayiladuthurai district; the nearest rail head is Mayiladuthurai, with local buses and taxis to the village.
